title: Syria's 'Barrel Bomb Mufti' Sentenced to Life for War Crimes
excerpt: Ahmad Badreddin Hassoun, Syria's former Grand Mufti who provided religious cover for the Assad regime's atrocities, was convicted after a six-day trial in Damascus.
body:
• Ahmad Badreddin Hassoun, Syria's former Grand Mufti, was sentenced to life imprisonment on August 24 by a Damascus criminal court
  • Hassoun was convicted of incitement to murder, abuse of office, and complicity in war crimes and crimes against humanity during the Syrian civil war
  • Prosecutors had sought the death penalty; the trial, which began on June 25, lasted six days before the Fourth Criminal Court
  • The verdict follows the earlier sentencing of Bashar al-Assad and seven other officials to death in absentia on August 11

The Verdict

A Damascus court sentenced Ahmad Badreddin Hassoun to life imprisonment on Monday for his role in providing religious legitimacy to the Assad regime's brutal crackdown during Syria's 13-year civil war. The ruling by the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus marks one of the most significant convictions in Syria's emerging transitional justice process.

https://x.com/AJEnglish/status/2091934950366851494

Hassoun, 77, served as Syria's Grand Mufti from 2005 to 2021 — the country's highest-ranking Sunni Muslim religious authority. Syrians gave him the epithet "barrel bomb mufti" for his fervent defense of the regime's use of indiscriminate barrel bombs against civilian areas, which he publicly described as "liberation."

The Case Against Him

The prosecution's case centered not on Hassoun as a direct perpetrator of violence, but as someone who conferred religious and moral legitimacy upon the regime's mass atrocities. He faced charges of incitement to murder, abuse of his position as Grand Mufti, justifying violence, and complicity in war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Evidence presented during the trial included recordings of sermons Hassoun delivered to Syrian Army personnel urging violence against opposition areas, public statements threatening residents of Idlib governorate with death or displacement, and his praise of foreign military commanders involved in operations against Syrian civilians.

"A system of atrocities isn't composed only of those who carry out its violence; it also includes those who confer legitimacy upon that violence."

— Syrian Network for Human Rights analysis of the trial

According to Amnesty International, Hassoun was deputized by Assad to approve prisoner executions at the notorious Sednaya prison north of Damascus, where the regime killed thousands through torture and starvation. Between 2012 and 2017, he reportedly approved the executions of 13,000 inmates. In 2017, he issued a fatwa explicitly authorizing the execution of Sednaya detainees.

From Interfaith Dialogue to War Crimes

Hassoun's trajectory traced a dramatic arc. Before Syria's uprising began in 2011, he was known internationally for promoting interfaith dialogue. In 2008, he addressed the European Parliament, declaring "there is no holy war, because a war can never be holy: it is peace that is holy."

That stance reversed sharply when protests erupted against Assad. Hassoun publicly threatened European countries in a 2011 televised speech, warning that if they attacked Syria, the country would train its citizens to become suicide bombers. He praised Iranian Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Soleimani and openly supported Russian and Iranian military intervention.

Assad abolished the Grand Mufti position without explanation in 2021, reportedly after Hassoun fell out of favor due to business ties with Assad's estranged billionaire cousin, Rami Makhlouf.

Arrest and Trial

When Assad's government fell in December 2024, Hassoun went into hiding. He was arrested at Damascus International Airport in March 2025 while attempting to board a flight to Amman, Jordan. The trial, presided over by the Fourth Criminal Court which handles transitional justice cases, began on June 25, 2026.

Prosecutors had sought the death penalty. The presiding judge, Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan, had himself defected to the Syrian opposition in 2013 and been sentenced to death by the Assad regime — an irony that underscored the dramatic reversal of power in post-Assad Syria.

A Broader Reckoning

The conviction follows a landmark ruling on August 11, when the same court sentenced Bashar al-Assad, his brother Maher, former defense minister Fahd Jassem al-Freij, and five other officials to death in absentia for premeditated murder, torture, and crimes against humanity. The Assad brothers fled to Russia after rebels took Damascus in December 2024.

The Hassoun verdict tests a legal principle that international criminal law has long struggled with: how to hold accountable those who enable mass violence through discourse and institutional authority rather than direct orders or physical acts. Syria's transitional government, led by Ahmad al-Sharaa, established the National Commission for Transitional Justice in May 2025 — though critics note the process has focused exclusively on Assad-era officials, excluding abuses by non-state actors during the civil war.
nri_angle: The Syrian transitional justice process carries significance for the Indian diaspora, with India historically maintaining diplomatic ties with Syria and a small Indian community in the region affected by the civil war's fallout.
